newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM refuses to rule out tax reform.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM refuses to rule out tax reform.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Tuesday explicitly refused to rule out any future reform of the taxation system, a day after a poll showed a controversial proposal for a consumption tax was a vote winner.
"He said I'm not prepared to rule out altogether any future reform of the taxation system," a spokesman for the ruling Liberal-National coalition quoted Howard as telling government parliamentarians.
But Howard said any reforms would have to lead to job creation, a lifting of exports, enhance living standards and encourage national savings.
On Monday, the Bulletin newsweekly's Morgan poll showed 59 percent of voters it surveyed now favoured a goods and services tax (GST), compared with 56 percent a year ago.
The poll found those who opposed it had dropped to 31 percent from 37 percent a year earlier.

Howard said last week he believed that tax reform debate was needed, leaving the way open for the coalition government to adopt a GST policy in the lead-up to the next election, due to be held by early 1999.
The coalition was widely perceived to have lost the 1993 election because of plans to introduce a GST.
It ousted the 13-year-old Labor administration in March 1996 after dropping the tax and pledging not to introduce a GST in its first term.
But it has not ruled out such a tax in later terms and support for such a policy is escalating with even welfare groups now calling for an overhaul of the tax system.
A GST is a consumption or value-added tax and is paid by consumers when they buy a good or service.
Australia currently has a range of indirect taxes, including sales tax, that are applied patchily and at varying rates.
